ch10 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Jerry Walls's introduction opens with the film Shadowlands (the Oxford dons teasing Lewis about the fur coats in the wardrobe) to present Lewis as a part-time philosopher who taught philosophy at Oxford and presided over the Socratic Club. It previews the questions the Chronicles raise: truth versus illusion, whether might makes right, why be moral, what may be accepted on faith, whether more than one religion could be true, whether time flows differently in different worlds, and whether Eustace could become a dragon and still be the same person. It reassures Narnia fans that the essays enrich rather than ponderously distort ('gas') stories that should first be enjoyed on their own terms.

chapters.file: ch11 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
ch12 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Stephen Webb argues that Lewis gives hearing, not sight, the fundamental role in knowledge: the Dufflepuds choose invisibility over ugliness, the crew in the Dark Island hear nightmares they cannot see, and in The Magician's Nephew Aslan is heard singing before he is seen. Against A.J. Ayer's logical positivism, Webb develops a 'vocative philosophy of sound' in which meaning lives in voices: Jadis's destructive Deplorable Word versus Aslan's world-creating song, Uncle Andrew's tone-deafness to warranted authority, and Shasta in The Horse and His Boy learning who he is from the voice in the dark that answers 'Myself.'

chapters.file: ch13 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Kevin Kinghorn uses virtue epistemology (Sosa, Code) to solve the puzzle of why Uncle Andrew alone hears only roaring when Aslan sings Narnia into being: he fails all four intellectual virtues. He does not value truth for its own sake (unlike Frank the Cabby), indulges wishful thinking (like Edmund defending the Witch for Turkish Delight, or imagining Jadis fancies him), lets fear dictate belief (terror of the animals he has vivisected), and lacks Socratic self-knowledge, which the dragonized Eustace painfully acquires. A closing reading of Prince Caspian has each character's ability to see Aslan track their earlier trust in Lucy's testimony: sin blinds, and faith produces its own authenticating evidence.

chapters.file: ch14 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Thomas Senor turns the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (lying, mad, or telling the truth) into a general account of when to believe incredible testimony: weigh the testifier's reliability against how well the claim fits your background beliefs. He shows why Lucy's siblings should have believed her second report of Aslan in Prince Caspian, since by then talking animals and a resurrected Lion no longer clashed with what they knew, and then applies the framework to 'Julia's' report of hearing God, arguing that believing, disbelieving, or withholding rationally depends on the hearer's own background commitments. A footnote explains why Hume on miracles does not fit Lucy's case, since she claims no violation of natural law.

chapters.file: ch15 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.

chapters.file: ch16 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bruce Reichenbach recounts the failure of the Enlightenment quest for certainty from Descartes and Locke through Kant to the positivists, and argues that Lewis's Narnia instead models knowing as perspectival (the Stable door whose inside is bigger than its outside), value-laden (the Dwarfs' self-chosen dark paradigm that turns Aslan's feast into refuse and violets into stable litter), and personal (Lucy's unarguable knowledge that she has seen Aslan in Prince Caspian, read through Michael Polanyi's tacit knowledge). Kuhn's competing paradigms frame theism versus atheism, James's will to believe opens the chapter, and Plantinga's defeaters keep personal knowledge from collapsing into mere subjectivity.

chapters.file: ch17 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
ch18 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Laura Garcia assembles Narnian heroes: Jill, Eustace, and Puddleglum untying Rilian at likely lethal cost, Eustace hacking at the Sea Serpent, unarmed Shasta charging the lion to save Aravis, and Digory refusing the Witch's offer of the apple that could heal his dying mother. She asks whether egoist theories can explain such deeds and argues they cannot: Hobbes's disguised self-interest, Butler's and Paley's reward schemes, Hume's sympathy, and MacIntyre's identity-based interests all fall short. Only love of others for their own sake, and (for Jill and Digory) trust in Aslan's proven goodness, explains both the heroic choices and our admiration of them as supererogatory acts beyond the call of duty.

chapters.file: ch19 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Devin Brown uses Eustace, who dodges work on Dragon Island until he wakes as a dragon and discovers he would rather be hungry among human friends than comfortable alone, to contrast Epicurean hedonism and Tom Sawyer's work-avoidance with Mill's higher pleasures and the 'Sherlock Holmes philosophy of work.' Weighing Aristotle's contemplative life against Lewis's love of quests, he reads Father Christmas's tailored gifts and 'everyone must do what he can do best' as an Acorn Philosophy of Vocation with a Marxian 'from each according to his ability' echo, condemns wrong livelihoods like Governor Gumpas's slave trade, and closes on leisure and Aristotle's golden mean, which Lewis turns into 'golden extremes.'

chapters.file: ch20 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Tim Mosteller identifies Lewis's Tao from The Abolition of Man with Aquinas's Natural Law, an objective moral order knowable by all rational beings, and maps three responses onto Narnian characters: wholehearted acceptance (Peter, Lucy, Tirian, Reepicheep), selective 'Innovators' who pick and choose (Shift and Miraz, with Nietzsche's invented master-values as the philosophical extreme), and total rejection by 'Conditioners' (Ginger the Cat, who reverts to dumb beast, and Uncle Andrew, who loses the animals' speech). Individual laws are illustrated by Mr. Tumnus freeing Lucy, Aslan scratching Aravis for her gladness at the slave girl's beating, Nikabrik's treacherous Realpolitik, Lucy's eavesdropping spell in the Magician's book, and Jill's showing-off at the cliff.

chapters.file: ch21 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bill Davis argues that Narnia works as a classical moral-education environment: against Experiment House's science-worship, Narnia supplies the three ingredients Aristotle and Aquinas require, namely instruction, virtuous exemplars to imitate (Reepicheep's courage, Puddleglum's temperance), and habituation through repeated right action, which together transform Peter's indecision, Edmund's treachery, Lucy's envy, and Jill's timidity. What finally lasts beyond Narnia, he contends, is a transforming encounter with Aslan: Eustace's dragon skin torn off by the Lion, Jill's drink at the stream where 'there is no other stream,' and Digory's tearful confession. He closes by arguing today's self-esteem-based character education cannot replicate this, since it pursues virtue from love of self rather than love of the good.

chapters.file: ch22 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Janice Daurio sets Plato's Thrasymachus and Callicles and Nietzsche's immoralism against three Narnian immoralists: Uncle Andrew, who exempts 'profound students and great thinkers' from rules meant for little boys, servants, and women; Queen Jadis, whose Deplorable Word and 'What else were they there for but to do my will?' embody might-makes-right; and the Green Witch, who extends going beyond good and evil to going beyond truth itself. Following Lewis's moral realism (the Golden Rule and Natural Law as facts like gravity, with Hobbes's lesson that someone always turns up with more power), she shows the immoralists cannot live by their own creed, since Uncle Andrew resents being treated as Jadis's slave, and since Lewis ties real authority to service, as when humble Frank the Cabby is made king.

chapters.file: ch23 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Gayne Anacker defines moral imagination, the capacity to see one's values and life from fresh moral perspectives, and argues the Chronicles exercise it through three character types readers live through: flawed repenters (Edmund, Eustace, Bree, Aravis), the essentially good under trial (Lucy believing her Aslan sighting in Prince Caspian, Caspian's greed on Goldwater Island), and the fatally self-absorbed (Uncle Andrew, Shift), together with portrayals of worship and of true versus usurped nobility (Peter versus Miraz). Philosophically he contends the stories' effectiveness supports virtue ethics over action-centered modern theories, and that disagreement among ethical theorists is no ground for relativism: no one needs theoretical consensus to know Miraz is evil.

chapters.file: ch24 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Wendy Hamblet asks whether Narnia feeds children a dangerous militaristic moral imaginary: Homeric warrior heroes, swarthy Calormene villains, voiceless animals excluded from moral concern, and battles that decide truth, in a lineage running from Plato's censorship of nursery stories through Descartes's modernity to Heidegger's seduction by Hitler's myths. On closer reading she finds Lewis undermining militarism: morally mixed characters, condemnation of aggression, despotism, and 'reasons of state,' and room only for just war and righteous self-defense. The finale is read through Plato's cave, as the Last Battle's worlds-within-worlds expose our political 'truths' as shadow-images that unscrupulous leaders manipulate when the god is absent.

holes.name: The Primacy of Sound (vocative philosophy)
holes.what: The view that meaning and knowledge are grounded in the human voice and hearing rather than in sight or silent text.
holes.why: Chapter 12 argues Lewis makes sound the fundamental sense: Narnia is created by Aslan's song, evil begins with a bell and a spoken word, and truth is heard before it is seen.

holes.name: Logical Positivism (verificationism)
holes.what: The doctrine, associated with A.J. Ayer, that only logically true or empirically verifiable statements are meaningful, making metaphysics and theology meaningless.
holes.why: Chapter 12 sets Lewis's voice-centered theory of truth against the logical positivism that dominated philosophy when he wrote the Chronicles.

holes.name: Virtue Epistemology
holes.what: A theory of knowledge, launched by Ernest Sosa and developed by Lorraine Code, that defines justification through intellectual virtues such as valuing truth and knowing one's limits.
holes.why: Chapter 13 explains why Uncle Andrew alone cannot hear the Talking Animals: he lacks the intellectual virtues a responsible seeker of knowledge needs.

holes.name: Epistemology of Testimony
holes.what: The study of when a hearer is justified in believing a speaker's report, based on the speaker's reliability and the fit of the claim with background beliefs.
holes.why: Chapter 14 builds its whole argument from the Professor's defense of Lucy's wardrobe story and applies the resulting principles to reports of religious experience.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who argued that belief in God is an illusion born of infantile helplessness and the longing for a protecting father.
holes.why: Chapter 15 reads the Green Witch's claim that the sun and Aslan are childish copies as a direct parallel to Freud's critique of religion, which the chapter then rebuts.

holes.name: The Genetic Fallacy
holes.what: The error of rejecting a belief as false solely because of its psychological or cultural origin.
holes.why: Chapter 15 answers the Freudian wish-fulfillment critique by naming the genetic fallacy: a belief's origin in desire does not show it is false.

holes.name: Michael Polanyi
holes.what: Philosopher-scientist who argued that all knowing is a personal commitment guided by tacit knowledge: we know more than we can tell.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Polanyi's personal knowledge to interpret Lucy's unsharable certainty that she has seen Aslan and knows his face's intent.

holes.name: Moral Imagination
holes.what: The capacity to see one's own values, choices, and life from fresh moral perspectives, a power that stories and literature exercise.
holes.why: Chapter 23 argues the Chronicles work by moral imagination, moving readers through identification with Edmund's repentance, Lucy's tested faith, and Uncle Andrew's deformity of self-absorption.

holes.name: The Moral Imaginary
holes.what: The culturally transmitted stock of images, heroes, and monsters in a community's stories that shapes children's sense of good and evil.
holes.why: Chapter 24 asks whether Narnia's heroic and monstrous imagery breeds militarism and ethnocentrism in the young or, read closely, undermines them.
